article_title: The Efficacy of Different Types of Metalinguistic Information in L2 Written Corrective Feedback
citation: Jang, Sung-Soo. (2020). The efficacy of different types of metalinguistic information in L2 written corrective feedback. English Teaching, 75(4), 33-56. https://doi.org/10.15858/engtea.75.4.202012.33
title: Pair written corrective feedback with immediate post-CF meaningful writing to convert explicit gains into implicit knowledge.
description: The article argues that written CF alone develops explicit knowledge, and that implicit knowledge develops only when learners immediately practice CF-targeted structures in a subsequent meaningful writing task. It states that "offering not only written CF but also subsequent opportunities for writing is required to develop learners' implicit knowledge beyond explicit knowledge", and that timely engagement was crucially responsible for the observed implicit gains.
requirements: A new piece of writing on CF-targeted structures must be carried out immediately after learners examine the written CF.
constraints: The contribution of post-CF writing for implicit knowledge may be restricted by its timing, per the immediacy finding the article cites from Chandler (2003).
target_learning_goals: Implicit knowledge of targeted grammatical structures (English article usage)
examples: In the experiment, the second dictogloss writing was carried out right after learners examined written CF on their first writing, and the DR, MS and MN groups showed implicit knowledge gains on the immediate posttest.
key_sources: Jang, Sung-Soo. (2020). The efficacy of different types of metalinguistic information in L2 written corrective feedback. English Teaching, 75(4), 33-56. https://doi.org/10.15858/engtea.75.4.202012.33

article_title: Conducting Implementation Research in Impact Studies of Education Interventions: A Guide for Researchers
citation: Hill, C. J., Scher, L., Haimson, J., & Granito, K. (2023). Conducting Implementation Research in Impact Studies of Education Interventions: A Guide for Researchers. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/
title: Conduct implementation analyses within impact studies so educators can judge local fit
description: The guide's rationale is that implementation analyses conducted as part of impact studies serve adoption decisions: they 'can help educators know whether a tested intervention is likely to be a good fit for their own settings'. Because impacts alone do not reveal what delivery conditions produced them, embedding implementation research gives practitioners the information needed to judge transferability to their contexts.
requirements: Impact studies should incorporate implementation analyses for their findings to inform local adoption decisions.
target_learning_goals: Judge whether an evidence-based intervention fits a local setting
examples: The guide was written to help researchers design and conduct these kinds of analyses within impact studies.
key_sources: Hill, C. J., Scher, L., Haimson, J., & Granito, K. (2023). Conducting Implementation Research in Impact Studies of Education Interventions: A Guide for Researchers. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/

article_title: Connecting SEERNet and Improvement Science to Pursue Better Outcomes in Schools
citation: Manai, J., & Roschelle, J. (2024, November). Connecting SEERNet and Improvement Science to Pursue Better Outcomes in Schools. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/234
title: Combining Improvement Science with SEERNet data capabilities as complementary engine and framework
description: The paper's central pattern pairs what it calls an "engine of improvement" — SEERNet's data and malleability of digital learning platforms — with Improvement Science as "a broader framework to keep the improvements accountable to important school challenges and educators' wisdom". SEERNet supplies learning-process data and rapid comparative testing; Improvement Science contributes problem identification, root-cause analysis, and iterative refinement via NICs and PDSA cycles, so interventions are both theoretically sound and practically applicable.
requirements: Collaboration between researchers and practitioners, with clear data-sharing protocols and professional development for interpreting platform data
constraints: Most SEERNet research questions to date have come from scientific theories and may not address educators' most pressing challenges; Integration requires addressing data privacy and security
target_learners: Students in schools and districts using digital learning platforms
target_learning_goals: Precise identification of student needs and continuous, scalable improvement of interventions
examples: A district uses SEERNet data showing uneven math performance to prompt systematic inquiry into causes and to test alternative solutions with data close to the learning process
key_sources: Manai, J., & Roschelle, J. (2024, November). Connecting SEERNet and Improvement Science to Pursue Better Outcomes in Schools. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/234

article_title: Improving Ed-Tech Purchasing
citation: Improving Ed-Tech Purchasing: Identifying the key obstacles and potential solutions for the discovery and acquisition of K-12 personalized learning tools. (2015). Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org/marketplace
title: Improve ed-tech procurement through formal needs assessment, better discovery infrastructure, structured pilots, and trusted evidence mechanisms
description: The brief recommends that schools and districts "conduct formal instructional needs assessments to more clearly define challenges" and publicize needs so providers can match them; that discovery be eased through RFIs and an online "Ed-tech Product Information Exchange"; that pilots be structured to generate efficacy evidence and a data-driven go or no-go decision; and that faster, cheaper evidence alternatives such as formal pilots, case studies, and small comparison-group designs bridge the evidence gap.
requirements: Districts need structured processes for assessing instructional needs and evaluating evidence
Trusted third parties or brokers are needed to verify effectiveness claims both sides accept
constraints: Most districts will not have resources to pay external consultants for vendor-relationship management, and digital platforms and brokers are not yet widespread in the ed-tech market
Evidence alternatives must not reduce instructional time or burden teachers
target_learners: K-12 students and teachers in U.S. public school districts
target_learning_goals: Access to personalized learning technology tools that meet identified instructional needs
examples: The brief recommends designing RFPs to focus on specific instructional needs rather than product features, creating collaborative purchasing guidelines including piggyback contracts, and researching pay-for-success approaches for the ed-tech market.
key_sources: Improving Ed-Tech Purchasing: Identifying the key obstacles and potential solutions for the discovery and acquisition of K-12 personalized learning tools. (2015). Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org/marketplace

article_title: ATS Hub Field Note — Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education
citation: Higgins, E. & Griffiths, R. (2026). ATS Field Note: Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education. ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/312
title: Collect implementation integrity and cross-context data, including how impact holds when implementation quality varies
description: Teams should gather data on implementation integrity and variability across contexts, addressing both whether a solution is implemented as intended and how it performs across a wide range of contexts. They should also "document the factors that support high quality implementation as well as the robustness of a breakthrough solution's impact on learning when implementation quality varies," for example under resource and staffing constraints.
requirements: Data collection on implementation integrity and contextual variability throughout development and evaluation
constraints: Implementation quality may vary due to resource and staffing constraints
target_learners: education R&D teams and implementation partners
target_learning_goals: robust solution performance across diverse implementation contexts
examples: The note gives resource and staffing constraints as an example source of implementation quality variation

article_title: How Individual Plans of Study Can Support Students’ College and Career Readiness and Success
citation: REL Central. (2023). How Individual Plans of Study Can Support Students’ College and Career Readiness and Success. REL Central. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/rel/regions/central/
title: Implement individual learning plans with adult support and regular review
description: This principle holds that personalized education and career plans work best when they are not stand-alone documents: the publication states that benefits are suggested "when IPS are implemented with the support of adults and regularly reviewed". Adults help students develop and use the plans, and periodic review keeps the plan aligned with the student’s evolving interests, skills, and goals throughout secondary school.
requirements: Support of adults during implementation
Plans are regularly reviewed rather than created once and left static
constraints: The publication suggests this practice may support outcomes; it does not report direct evidence of effectiveness
target_learning_goals: college and career readiness
academic engagement
sense of agency
examples: The publication frames IPS as plans that guide and focus students’ efforts throughout middle and high school when supported and reviewed by adults

article_title: The Promise of Micro-credentials and Learning and Employment Record Technologies for Youth and K-12 Schools
citation: Zohal Shah, Marilys Galindo, Chioma Aso-Hernandez, Christina Luke Luna, Keun-woo Lee, Josh Weisgrau, Teresa Solorzano, Britney Jacobs. (2024). The Promise of Micro-credentials and Learning and Employment Record Technologies for Youth and K-12 Schools. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Implementation science framework for assessing district readiness
description: The report grounds its conceptual framework in implementation science, a model for understanding how educational interventions are adopted and scaled that focuses on "fidelity, feasibility, and sustainability" rather than real-time effectiveness. Following McKay (2017), the authors examine contextual factors affecting a district's readiness to implement competency-based micro-credentials and LER technologies while centering HSE learners, identifying indicators such as community or institutional partnerships, data privacy and infrastructure, and student advising and career support. This yields a Readiness Framework (Appendix B) for district leaders.
requirements: Fostering and sustaining partnerships with districts, universities, community organizations, and workforce organizations
Intervention must match the needs of the target population and be possible to implement in the given context
constraints: Without technical assistance or research-practice partnership support, conditions for implementation in schools are often not ideal
target_learners: K-12 students in partner districts, especially HSE learners
target_learning_goals: Recognition of competencies through micro-credentials and LER technologies
examples: The team used the framework's criteria to select two districts for pilot planning and refined it through listening tours and cross-sector design sessions.

article_title: Solving the Teacher Shortage: How to Attract and Retain Excellent Educators
citation: Podolsky, A., Kini, T., Bishop, J., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2016). Solving the Teacher Shortage: How to Attract and Retain Excellent Educators. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/solving-teacher-shortage
title: Improve working conditions—leadership, collaboration, and resources—because they define learning conditions and drive retention
description: The report argues that "Teaching conditions—which also define learning conditions for students—are a strong predictor of teachers' decisions about where to teach and whether to stay." It recommends investing in high-quality principals who include teachers in decision-making, surveying teachers about the teaching and learning environment (e.g., the TELL survey), and redesigning schedules and resources to enable sustained teacher collaboration, which improves efficacy and retention.
requirements: Sustained collaboration requires changes in scheduling and resource allocation so teachers have time for productive collaboration
constraints: The report cautions that one policy in isolation will do little; working-condition improvements should be part of a mutually reinforcing policy set
target_learners: teachers in high-need schools and the principals and district leaders who shape their working environments
target_learning_goals: improving teacher retention and the quality of teaching and learning conditions in schools
examples: The TELL survey asks about school culture, principal leadership, and collegial relationships that predict job satisfaction and career plans
Effective principal preparation programs include problem-based learning, field-based internships, cohort groups, and district collaboration

article_title: The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad
citation: Gupta, K. (2026). The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10609387/v1
title: Immersion heuristic: crossing AI support with human engagement to target supported immersion
description: A two-by-two diagnostic aid for programme designers crossing AI support (low/high) with human engagement (low/high). The four cells are unmanaged struggle, traditional immersion, frictionless enclosure and supported immersion. "The target condition is supported immersion, not minimal technology." The heuristic also clarifies why volume of AI use is theoretically weak as a measure: two students may use AI equally often, one to prepare for and reflect on daily host-community interactions, the other to avoid them.
requirements: AI support and human engagement must be treated as varying independently when designing programmes
constraints: Offered as a diagnostic aid rather than as a further theoretical construct
target_learning_goals: host-community interaction
supported participation without frictionless enclosure
examples: Table 2 describes frictionless enclosure as AI translating, interpreting, reassuring and solving problems while host-community interaction remains limited

article_title: Implementation Intentions and Goal Achievement: A Meta‐analysis of Effects and Processes
citation: Gollwitzer, Peter M., Sheeran, Paschal. (2006). Implementation intentions and goal achievement: a meta-analysis of effects and processes. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 38, 69-119. https://nbn-resolving.de/urn:nbn:de:bsz:352-opus-56534
title: Implementation intentions as if-then plans that specify the when, where, and how of goal striving in advance
description: The article defines an implementation intention as a plan that "spells out the when, where, and how of goal striving in advance" in the format "If situation Y is encountered, then I will initiate goal-directed behavior X!". The framework holds that strong goal intentions alone do not guarantee achievement because people may fail to deal effectively with self-regulatory problems during goal striving; implementation intentions address this by pre-linking a critical situation to a goal-directed response, which the meta-analysis links to enhanced cue accessibility and automated responding.
requirements: A specified critical situation (when/where) and a specified goal-directed response (how) must be linked in an if-then format formed in advance of goal striving.
target_learners: individuals pursuing personal or task goals
target_learning_goals: goal attainment and self-regulation of goal striving

article_title: Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks
citation: Nilsen P. (2015). Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks. Implementation Science. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13012-015-0242-0
title: Implementation theories: theories developed or adapted by implementation researchers to explain implementation
description: The fourth category comprises theories developed by implementation researchers, from scratch or by adapting existing theories and concepts, to provide understanding and/or explanation of aspects of implementation. Examples include Implementation Climate, Absorptive Capacity, Organizational Readiness, COM-B and Normalization Process Theory. Adaptation "allows researchers to prioritize aspects considered to be most critical", improving relevance to particular circumstances. COM-B posits that capability, opportunity and motivation generate behaviour, which in turn influences the three components; Normalization Process Theory identifies four determinants of embedding complex interventions in practice.
requirements: Adaptation of existing theories should prioritize aspects most critical to analysing the how and why of implementation
target_learning_goals: understanding mechanisms of implementation and embedding of interventions in practice
examples: Normalization Process Theory began as a model based on empirical studies of implementing new technologies and was later developed into a theory
key_sources: Nilsen P. (2015). Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks. Implementation Science. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13012-015-0242-0

article_title: A Reconsideration of Cognitive Load Theory
citation: Schnotz, W., Kürschner, C. (2007). A Reconsideration of Cognitive Load Theory. Educational Psychology Review 19, 469–508. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9053-4
title: Implicit learning perspective on cognitive load theory
description: The article also reconsiders cognitive load theory "from the perspective of research on implicit learning". Because implicit learning can proceed without deliberate, load-bearing processing, high deliberate load does not necessarily prevent learning, which further undermines the assumption that reducing load always benefits learning.
requirements: A theory of instructional load must account for implicit as well as explicit learning mechanisms
target_learners: learners acquiring skills implicitly, including complex skill domains
target_learning_goals: implicit acquisition of patterns and skills

article_title: Fitness, physical activity and academic achievement in overweight/obese children
citation: Cadenas-Sanchez, C., Migueles, J. H., Esteban-Cornejo, I., Mora-Gonzalez, J., Henriksson, P., Rodriguez-Ayllon, M., Molina-García, P., Löf, M., Labayen, I., Hillman, C. H., Catena, A., & Ortega, F. B. (2020). Fitness, physical activity, and academic achievement in overweight/obese children. Journal of Sports Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/02640414.2020.1729516
title: Public health strategies should improve multiple aspects of fitness, not only cardiorespiratory fitness, to support academic achievement in children with overweight/obesity
description: The article recommends that interventions and public health strategies target the full set of health-related fitness components rather than cardiorespiratory fitness alone. The authors state that "public health strategies should focus on improving multiple aspects of fitness as an effective approach to enhance academic achievement in children", grounded in their finding that muscular strength and speed-agility, alongside cardiorespiratory fitness, were positively associated with academic outcomes in children with overweight/obesity. The recommendation is framed as requiring verification by future randomized controlled trials.
requirements: Future randomized controlled trials are needed to verify the cross-sectional associations before causal claims can be made
constraints: The supporting evidence is cross-sectional and cannot draw causality
Most fitness associations attenuated or disappeared after adjustment for BMI and cardiorespiratory fitness
The limited sample size, especially in the 1-RM or school grade outcomes, reduces the power of the analyses
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement including language, mathematics, and science skills
examples: The ActiveBrains project, a randomized controlled trial of a 20-week physical activity intervention in children with overweight/obesity, within which this baseline analysis was conducted

article_title: Improved probabilistic inference as a general learning mechanism with action video games
citation: Green, C.S., Pouget, A., & Bavelier, D. (2010). Improved probabilistic inference as a general learning mechanism with action video games. Current Biology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2010.07.040
title: Improved probabilistic inference as a general mechanism explaining broad transfer from action video-game play
description: The article proposes that action video-game play improves the nervous system's use of noisy sensory evidence: players learn the statistics of the task's stimuli and accumulate evidence more efficiently, yielding "a more accurate posterior distribution" over choices. Because evidence-accumulation circuits are argued to be shared or multimodal across modalities, this single mechanism explains why game training transfers to widely different tasks. The authors suggest the mechanism "may serve as a signature of training regimens that are likely to produce transfer of learning."
requirements: Training must involve situations that are rarely repeated, so learners must extract stimulus statistics on the fly rather than a task-specific solution
constraints: The authors state they can only speculate about the neural mechanisms of the transfer, listing shared accumulation circuits, fronto-parietal networks, and neuromodulator release as open possibilities for future work
target_learners: young adults with and without action video-game experience
target_learning_goals: probabilistic inference and efficient accumulation of noisy sensory evidence across visual and auditory tasks
key_sources: Green, C.S., Pouget, A., & Bavelier, D. (2010). Improved probabilistic inference as a general learning mechanism with action video games. Current Biology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2010.07.040

article_title: Children's Effortful Control and Academic Achievement: Mediation Through Social Functioning
citation: Valiente Carlos, Eisenberg Nancy, Haugen Rg, Spinrad Tracy L., Hofer Claire, Liew Jeffrey, Kupfer Anne. (2011). Children's Effortful Control and Academic Achievement: Mediation Through Social Functioning. Early Education and Development, 22(3), 411-433. https://doi.org/10.1080/10409289.2010.505259
title: Support children's effortful control development because it yields both social and academic advantages
description: The article recommends that educators and curriculum developers consider students' social and emotional functioning in models of school success, and that "a focused effort to improve EC is advantageous because growth in this area is likely to produce both social advantages (e.g., high levels of social competence and low levels of problem behaviors) and academic advantages." Many self-regulation activities are described as relatively inexpensive or free and classroom-administrable. Administrators are advised to give teachers clear messages supporting the modest time needed for such activities.
requirements: Administrators need to provide clear messages supporting the modest amount of time needed to promote students' EC for teachers to engage in such activities
constraints: The article cites mounting evidence that attentional abilities and inhibitory control can be improved via training, but this study itself is longitudinal-correlational, not an intervention trial
target_learners: children in preschool programs and elementary schools
target_learning_goals: self-regulation, social competence, and academic achievement
examples: The authors point to interventions such as the Head Start REDI program and the preschool PATHS curriculum as evidence that EC-related skills can be improved

description: The Image Processing for Teaching (IPT) project at the University of Arizona is the second of three educational examples the article provides of "using scientific visualization within education." It applies image-processing tools as a vehicle for learners to engage in scientific visualization practices in classroom settings.
requirements: Classroom access to image-processing software and suitable image data

article_title: A framework for infrastructuring sustainable innovations in education
citation: Chen, B. (2024). A framework for infrastructuring sustainable innovations in education. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2024.2320159
title: The IMPROV framework: six interconnected action areas for infrastructuring sustainable educational innovations
description: The IMPROV framework organizes infrastructuring in education into six interconnected action areas: identifying key social actors and design areas, making visible existing infrastructures, planning possible points of infrastructuring, rallying for coherence-making and infrastructure remaking, orchestrating meta-design and capacity building, and evaluating infrastructures continually. The article states it "oWers actionable guidance on infrastructuring in the learning sciences and education in six interconnected action areas." Its core claim is that sustaining an innovation requires revealing components of existing infrastructures and nurturing stakeholder coherence-making between the innovation and those infrastructures.
requirements: Work in the six areas may occur in parallel or move back-and-forth; the framework requires flexibly responding to emergent needs of the innovation rather than following a strict sequence
constraints: Strategies developed in other disciplines need revisions or new strategies to address persistent problems in education settings, given education's entrenched beliefs, norms, and structures
target_learners: educators and practitioners across K-12 and higher education
target_learning_goals: sustaining learning innovations in authentic educational settings
building capacity for practitioner-led design
examples: The framework is illustrated with examples from Knowledge Building initiatives, including the IdeaMagnets project in a US public school and KB work in a Toronto laboratory school
key_sources: Chen, B. (2024). A framework for infrastructuring sustainable innovations in education. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2024.2320159

article_title: Mobile augmented reality supporting families’ immersive collaborative learning: Learning-on-the-move for place-based geoscience sense-making
citation: Heather Toomey Zimmerman, Susan M. Land, Lillyanna Faimon, Yu-Chen Chiu. (2023). Mobile augmented reality supporting families’ immersive collaborative learning: Learning-on-the-move for place-based geoscience sense-making. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09399-9
title: Immersive, family-centered, place-based LOTM framework linking the five SANSE immersion processes to mobile augmented reality design conjectures
description: The article contributes a design framework combining learning-on-the-move with Enyedy and Yoon's five-part immersion framework, called SANSE: "sensory, actional, narrative, social, and emancipatory" immersion. These immersive processes are operationalized as design conjectures (Table 2) specifying how MAR features—prompts, filters, GPS wayfinding, photo-taking—support intergenerational family sense-making about geologic time in outdoor informal settings. Each conjecture pairs the immersion category with Time Explorers examples, grounding XR-time-travel narratives in learners' physical place.
requirements: A place-based outdoor setting with physical specimens or exhibits the app content can connect to
A mobile augmented reality app delivering content triggered by GPS location or markers
constraints: The article found no substantial example of emancipatory immersion from its own data
target_learners: Intergenerational families with children aged 5–12 in informal outdoor settings
target_learning_goals: Understanding geologic time scale and land–water geoscience processes through collaborative place-based sense-making
examples: Time Explorers sent families walking a time-spiral sculpture, walking an AR-underwater-filtered coral sculpture, and estimating a stalagmite's age to fix a fictional time machine across eight microsites

article_title: Effects of immersion in inquiry-based learning on student teachers’ educational beliefs
citation: Voet, M. & De Wever, B. (2018). Effects of immersion in inquiry-based learning on student teachers' educational beliefs. Instructional Science, 46(3), 383-403. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-017-9439-8
title: Immersion in inquiry-based learning ('teach as you preach') as a professional development approach
description: Professional development on IBL commonly applies the teaching-as-you-preach principle: putting teachers through a substantive inquiry experience mirroring what they should do in class. The article states this roots in social learning theory, in which behaviors are "learned, either deliberately or inadvertently, through the influence of example". Rather than delivering information, immersion provides teachers with good practices they observe and potentially adopt.
requirements: Teachers work through a substantive amount of content in a way that mirrors the target pedagogical approach
constraints: Some scholars argue immersion may fail without meta-commentary making underlying ideas explicit
target_learning_goals: shifting teachers' educational beliefs toward inquiry-based learning
increasing self-efficacy for inquiry
examples: 302 student history teachers completed a four-hour WISE inquiry activity on the English Peasants' Revolt of 1381

article_title: Measuring cognitive load with subjective rating scales during problem solving: differences between immediate and delayed ratings
citation: Schmeck, A., Opfermann, M., van Gog, T., Paas, F., & Leutner, D. (2015). Measuring cognitive load with subjective rating scales during problem solving: differences between immediate and delayed ratings. Instructional Science, 43, 93–114. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-014-9328-3
title: Treat immediate (per-task) and delayed (post-sequence) subjective cognitive load ratings as distinct, non-interchangeable measures
description: When using subjective rating scales to measure cognitive load, researchers should not assume that the average of ratings given after each task equals a single rating given after the whole learning phase. Across two experiments, "the delayed ratings of both effort and difﬁculty were signiﬁcantly higher than the average of the six ratings made during problem solving", while affective ratings showed no such difference. The choice of measurement point therefore changes what the rating indicates and should be reported and justified.
requirements: Researchers must decide and report whether ratings are collected after each task or once after the whole phase, since the two yield systematically different cognitive load values.
constraints: The evidence comes from short sequences of six weekday-problems with teacher education students; the article notes it remains unclear what exactly a single delayed rating indicates (average, recency, or most complex tasks).
target_learning_goals: valid measurement of cognitive load during learning and problem solving
examples: In both experiments, students rated mental effort, perceived difficulty, interest and motivation after each of six problems and again once after the whole sequence, allowing direct comparison of the two approaches.
key_sources: Schmeck, A., Opfermann, M., van Gog, T., Paas, F., & Leutner, D. (2015). Measuring cognitive load with subjective rating scales during problem solving: differences between immediate and delayed ratings. Instructional Science, 43, 93–114. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-014-9328-3

article_title: Collaborative design as a form of professional development
citation: Joke Voogt, Therese Laferrière, Alain Breuleux, Rebecca C. Itow, Daniel T. Hickey, Susan McKenney (2015). Collaborative design as a form of professional development. Instr Sci (2015) 43:259-282. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-014-9340-7
title: Interconnected Model of Professional Growth (IMPG) as used to interpret teacher learning in teacher design teams
description: In Case 2, the article uses the Interconnected Model of Professional Growth (Clarke and Hollingsworth 2002) to understand teachers' learning in each teacher design team. The model "postulates that change can take place in any of four domains: the external domain, the personal domain, the domain of practice and the domain of consequences." External-domain change means becoming acquainted with new ideas and strategies introduced by others; personal-domain change is acquiring new knowledge, skills, attitudes or beliefs; practice-domain change arises from collaborative design and enactment; and consequence-domain change concerns outcomes for teachers and students. The model holds that "Change may occur in any domain and is mediated through the processes of reflection and enactment," and the case organizes its findings under these four domains.
requirements: Interpretation requires examining change in the four domains together, with reflection and enactment as the mediating processes.
target_learning_goals: understanding teacher professional growth during collaborative curriculum design
examples: In the African studies, kick-off workshops and TPACK framing served the external domain, while reflections on implemented lessons drove changes in technology integration approaches in the practice domain.

article_title: Does Embodiment in Virtual Reality Boost Learning Transfer? Testing an Immersion-Interactivity Framework
citation: Klingenberg, S., Bosse, R., Mayer, R. E., & Makransky, G. (2024). Does Embodiment in Virtual Reality Boost Learning Transfer? Testing an Immersion-Interactivity Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09956-0
title: Immersion-interactivity framework of embodiment
description: The article proposes a 2x2 framework of embodiment for virtual learning environments built on the taxonomies of Johnson-Glenberg et al. (2014) and Skulmowski and Rey (2018). The immersion dimension ranges from low-immersion desktop or tablet simulations to high-immersion HMD-based VR, and the interactivity dimension ranges from incidental gestures (e.g., a laser pointer) to congruent gestures relevant to the learning task. The authors state: "In the context of VR, we propose a 2 × 2 framework of embodiment based on immersion and interactivity, building on these taxonomies." Unlike Johnson-Glenberg's ranked taxonomy, it does not specify whether immersion or interactivity matters more, and it predicts the greatest embodiment when both are high.
requirements: A virtual learning environment whose immersion and interactivity levels can be independently varied so the four combinations can be instantiated
constraints: The framework does not specify whether immersion or interactivity has a greater impact, unlike the Johnson-Glenberg et al. (2014) ranking
target_learners: high school students learning procedural science skills
target_learning_goals: procedural knowledge and transfer of technical procedures
examples: The study instantiated the four cells as VR congruent, VR incidental, PC congruent, and PC incidental versions of a pipetting lesson

citation: Klingenberg, S., Bosse, R., Mayer, R. E., & Makransky, G. (2024). Does Embodiment in Virtual Reality Boost Learning Transfer? Testing an Immersion-Interactivity Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09956-0
title: Immersion principle: pair highly immersive media with instructional methods that amplify benefits and mitigate drawbacks
description: The article invokes the immersion principle in multimedia learning, which "proposes that people learn more effectively with highly immersive media when accompanied by effective instructional methods that amplify the benefits and mitigate the drawbacks of these technologies." It is used to argue that instructional design in immersive virtual lessons should reduce unnecessary extraneous load and keep learners focused on the content, since highly immersive and interactive experiences can either aid learning or act as seductive details depending on design.
requirements: Deliberate instructional design of the virtual lesson to reduce extraneous cognitive load
constraints: The article notes gesticulations can in some studies increase cognitive load and impair learning, so embodied interaction is not uniformly beneficial
target_learners: students learning in immersive VR environments
target_learning_goals: acquisition of factual, conceptual, and procedural knowledge and transfer
examples: The study's pre-registered predictions acknowledged that immersion and interactivity could serve as aids to learning or as seductive details that distract from learning in VR

article_title: Happy Together? On the Relationship Between Research on Retrieval Practice and Generative Learning Using the Case of Follow-Up Learning Tasks
citation: Julian Roelle, Tino Endres, Roman Abel, Niklas Obergassel, Matthias Nückles, Alexander Renkl. (2023). Happy Together? On the Relationship Between Research on Retrieval Practice and Generative Learning Using the Case of Follow-Up Learning Tasks. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09810-9
title: Reflect on each task's implementation quality when comparing retrieval practice, generative learning, or their combination
description: The review proposes that future research comparing retrieval practice, generative learning activities, or their combination must attend to how well each activity is implemented. It argues that in both research fields the other activity type has often been implemented in low quality, which limits what can be learned about their interaction, stating that in such comparisons "it is crucial to reflect on each task's implementation quality." This tenet is one of three the review offers for consolidating the relationship between the two research strands.
requirements: Comparisons should implement each task feature at adequate quality, e.g., retrieval practice with sufficient retrievability, repetition, and spacing
constraints: The review notes prior horse-race comparisons often pitted tasks of unequal implementation quality, making them uninformative
target_learners: researchers and designers of follow-up learning tasks
target_learning_goals: valid comparison of learning-task features and their combination
examples: The review cites Karpicke and Blunt (2011) as pitting a poorly implemented concept-mapping task against a well-implemented free-recall task

article_title: Benefits of Taking a Virtual Field Trip in Immersive Virtual Reality: Evidence for the Immersion Principle in Multimedia Learning
citation: Guido Makransky · Richard E. Mayer. (2022). Benefits of Taking a Virtual Field Trip in Immersive Virtual Reality: Evidence for the Immersion Principle in Multimedia Learning. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1771–1798. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09675-4
title: The immersion principle in multimedia learning
description: The immersion principle "proposes that immersive virtual environments promote better learning when they incorporate multimedia design principles" and holds that "immersive media per se do not necessarily improve learning". It predicts people learn better with immersive media (e.g., a 3D HMD video) than less immersive media when lessons follow instructional design principles and the affordances of the media. The article tests it with a media-comparison experiment in a real middle-school intervention, and the results support it.
requirements: Lessons must be designed according to instructional design principles and the affordances of the media, promoting selecting, organizing, and integrating information.
constraints: Higher immersion is not automatically beneficial; cognitive load, seductive details, distraction, and poor pedagogy are stated boundary conditions under which immersion can be counterproductive.
target_learning_goals: declarative science knowledge about climate change (greenhouse effect, albedo effect)
examples: The study implemented evidence-based design principles (multimedia, signaling, split attention, redundancy, modality, personalization) in both versions of the Greenland virtual field trip and compared HMD to 2D video within a six-lesson IBSL intervention.

citation: Lavrijsen, J., Vansteenkiste, M., Boncquet, M., & Verschueren, K. (2022). Does motivation predict changes in academic achievement beyond intelligence and personality? A multitheoretical perspective. JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY, 114(4), 772–790. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000666
title: Improving student motivation is a worthwhile undertaking because motivational dynamics are more malleable than intelligence and personality
description: The article recommends investing in student motivation on the grounds that motivational dynamics are more malleable than intelligence and personality differences, while motivation still carries unique, positive associations with achievement. It states that "the unique, positive associations between motivation and achievement suggest that improving student motivation is a worthwhile undertaking." The Educational Impact Statement adds that parents, teachers and schools could do well to promote motivation in students.
requirements: Motivation's unique association with achievement beyond intelligence and personality, as established in the study
constraints: The recommendation rests on predictive associations in one sample of Flemish seventh graders, not on a tested intervention

examples: The study controlled for intelligence and personality and found motivational constructs still explained about a quarter of the explained variance in school results

article_title: Foil type modulates developmental changes in statistical learning across childhood to adulthood
citation: Liang, F., Zhu, Y., Li, R. & Fu, Q. (2026). Foil Type Modulates Developmental Changes in Statistical Learning Across Childhood to Adulthood. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00434-6
title: Implicit-explicit competitive interaction account of developmental change in statistical learning
description: The article interprets its crossover pattern through the competitive neurocognitive networks framework, which "proposes that the interactions between implicit and explicit systems evolve across development." Implicit extraction of statistical regularities is described as most robust prior to age 12, supporting efficient discrimination of familiarized words from nonword foils, while adults' advantage on partword foils "likely involves additional involvement of explicit processes." Children may initially acquire a "fuzzy" representation of frequent patterns, with the ability to precisely delineate boundaries and suppress interference from overlapping partword foils continuing to mature into adulthood.
requirements: A 2AFC design that includes both nonword foils and partword foils, since the dissociation would be obscured if foil types were collapsed
constraints: The account is the authors' interpretation of a behavioral crossover pattern, not a directly tested mechanism; the study was behavioral-only and did not include adolescents
target_learning_goals: auditory statistical learning of word boundaries in continuous speech
examples: Grade 5 children outperformed younger children only on nonword foils, whereas adults selectively outperformed Grade 5 children on partword foils, the pattern the framework is invoked to explain

article_title: Understanding and supporting university students’ use of distributed practice via implementation intentions
citation: David, L., Biwer, F., Crutzen, R., & de Bruin, A. (2026). Understanding and supporting university students' use of distributed practice via implementation intentions. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00448-0
title: Implementation intentions as a metacognitive planning strategy linking situational cues to goal-directed study behaviour
description: Implementation intentions are specific plans that connect a situational cue to a goal-directed behaviour, extending a goal intention with a plan specifying when, where, and how to act. The article describes them as "a metacognitive strategy in which goal-achievement is supported by extending the goal intention with a detailed plan". In this study students in the intervention group specified when and how to incorporate regular review sessions and formulated if-then obstacle plans. The authors argue this structured planning could foster effective study habits, though the empirical test found no increase in distributed practice.
requirements: Plans must be specific enough to link cues to actions; the article reports many students struggled to specify components in detail, which could weaken the cue-context link.
constraints: Effects depend on plan quality, if-then format, and motivation; the four-week course may have been too short to capture behavioural change from goal refinement cycles.
target_learners: university students in health-related undergraduate programs
target_learning_goals: self-regulated use of distributed practice and effective learning strategies
examples: Students planned review via practice-testing, summarization, or visualization (e.g., flashcards after tutorials), scheduled at home or in the library, with obstacle plans for poor time-management and distractions.

citation: Minkang Kim, Jean Decety, Ling Wu, Soohyun Baek and Derek Sankey. (2021). Neural computations in children's third-party interventions are modulated by their parents' moral values. npj Science of Learning 6:38. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00116-5
title: Early implicit evaluation account of preschoolers' costly third-party intervention
description: This account holds that young children's costly intervention into third-party harm is driven by rapid implicit evaluation of moral norm violation rather than by late deliberative processes, impulsivity, or self-oriented distress. In it, early neural discrimination indexed by central P2 shapes later regulatory processing and the decision to intervene. The article states that "rapid implicit evaluations of norm violations are implicated in a young child 's intervention into third-party harm", and that late neural dynamics are bounded by earlier temporal dynamics.
requirements: Triangulated measurement combining EEG/ERP recordings, observed behaviour in a live transgression setting, and parent-report dispositions
constraints: The brain–behaviour relationships were drawn from group-level data
Due to the small sample size, analysis of the Protester group was underpowered
Children may have attributed power and authority to the adult transgressor, preventing protest or report
target_learning_goals: moral norm evaluation and costly third-party intervention into harm

citation: Emily Brooks, Sarah Wallis, Joshua Hendrikse & James Coxon. (2024). Micro-consolidation occurs when learning an implicit motor sequence, but is not influenced by HIIT exercise. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00238-6
title: Implicit serial reaction time task with 10-s alternating practice-rest structure for measuring micro-consolidation
description: An implicit serial reaction time task (SRTT) in which "the task alternated every 10-s between task practice and rest for a total of 16 practice blocks, 320-s in total". Participants respond to visual cues with four fingers of the non-dominant left hand; undisclosed to them, cues follow a 12-item repeating sequence (2-3-1-4-3-2-4-1-3-4-2-1). Skill is conceptualised as number of correct responses per second, and micro-offline and micro-online changes are computed from block-start and block-end tapping speeds using a four-item sliding average.
requirements: Correct response required to progress to the next cue; post-task questioning to detect explicit awareness of five or more sequence items
constraints: The 12-item sequence differs from the seminal explicit 5-item micro-consolidation work and from SRTT versions using fixed-versus-random comparison, limiting direct quantification of implicit learning magnitude
target_learning_goals: implicit motor sequence learning
examples: Used with 38 participants pseudo-randomly allocated to HIIT or LOW exercise conditions before task completion

article_title: A practical implementation science framework for education
citation: Allen, S. E., Bardach, L., Jirout, J., Mackey, A., McCoy, D., Pesando, L. M., & Kizilcec, R. F. (2026). A practical implementation science framework for education. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00430-w
title: Supplementary implementation toolkit: one-page overview, milestone checklist, SWOT-based Theory of Change brainstorming aid, and case studies
description: A set of simplified planning tools provided in the article's supplementary information, designed to avoid jargon and integrate existing frameworks. It includes "a one-page summary of the principles, processes, and pitfalls," "a checklist for planning and conducting an implementation project that is patterned after familiar pre-registration protocols" providing criteria for advancing between stages, "a brainstorming aid to help craft a Theory of Change" based on SWOT Analysis, and brief accounts of three well-documented case studies. The tools deliberately do not itemize every possible factor, instead ensuring planning is sufficiently thorough in finding factors to consider.

citation: Duan, R., Sun, Q., & Tong, X. (2025). Non-linear development in statistical learning of visual orthographic regularities. npj Science of Learning 10, 6. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00298-2
title: iMINERVA memory-based account of consistency-dependent statistical learning development
description: The article invokes the iMINERVA model, "a computational model accounting for distributional statistical learning" proposed by Thiessen and Pavlik Jr., which emphasizes long-term memory via "memory-based principles of similarity-based comparison, decay, integration, and abstraction". Under this account, learners compare prior and current pseudocharacters and integrate them into a consistent positional representation when consistency passes a threshold; integration facilitates learning at high and moderate consistency but is weakened at 60% consistency, and memory development with age yields different trajectories for more consistent levels.

constraints: The article presents this as an interpretation; it states the interplay of statistical learning development, memory, and prior language experience requires further tests to prove

distributional statistical learning
examples: The article uses iMINERVA to explain why high (100%) and moderate (80%) consistency showed developmental change while low (60%) consistency showed none, attributing the latter to constrained memory retrieval of conflicted representations

citation: Boels, L., Garcia Moreno-Esteva, E., Bakker, A., & Drijvers, P. (2024). title: Interpretable mathematical model (IMM) algorithm for classifying gaze strategies from saccade properties
description: The IMM is an algorithm that transforms sequences of saccades on the graph area into classifications of horizontal or vertical scanning. It maps saccades to values based on length (200-pixel cutoff) and slope (0.875 cutoff), removes short saccades, counts runs of consecutive long horizontal or vertical scans, and outputs a binary classification. The authors state "The best model we found relies on the following algorithm, which is based on saccade lengths and angles." Cut-off values were found empirically by testing values close to a slope of 1.

Prior qualitative identification of attentional anchors to set the starting point for slope cutoffs
constraints: The 200-pixel saccade length cutoff was fixed and not scaled to the width and height of the graph area
The model was constructed as one general model for all five histogram items based on similar attentional anchors across items
target_learning_goals: Automated identification of students' task-specific strategies for estimating the mean from histograms
examples: The algorithm maps saccades to -1, 0, or 1 values, splits into subsequences, removes duplicates and short saccades, and sums to determine predominantly horizontal or vertical scanning

citation: Duong Ngo, Andy Nguyen, Belle Dang, Ha Ngo. (2024). Facial Expression Recognition for Examining Emotional Regulation in Synchronous Online Collaborative Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 34:650–669. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00378-7
title: FER analysis pipeline combining img2pose facial localization and Residual Masking Network emotion detection for synchronous online learning video

constraints: The pipeline uses publicly available pre-trained models because the dataset scope (< 100 examples per class) makes training or fine-tuning domain-specific models impractical

title: Interconnected Model of Professional Growth (IMPG) as a framework for understanding technology-supported teacher professional development
description: The Interconnected Model of Professional Growth (Clarke & Hollingsworth, 2002) is the theoretical framework this study uses to understand how teachers develop skills and knowledge over time. It proposes teachers as active learners who shape their professional development through reflective participation in professional development programs and day-to-day practice. Professional development results from reflection and enactment across four interrelated domains: the external domain (external sources of information or support), the domain of practice (professional experimentation), the domain of consequences (salient outcomes such as student learning or motivation), and the personal domain (teacher knowledge, beliefs, and attitudes). Learning and growth occur when changes in one domain lead to changes in another through reflection and enactment.
requirements: Change in one domain must mediate to another through the processes of reflection and enactment
target_learning_goals: Understanding and supporting teacher professional development processes
examples: The study mapped teachers' TARGET-tool experiences onto the four domains, e.g., experimentation in the evaluation dimension producing an assessment rubric

description: The review proposes differentiating immersive and virtual patient technologies along three dimensions derived from the included reviews: "level of immersion", "interaction design", and "representational fidelity". constraints: The review notes the included reviews rarely differentiated clearly between levels of technological sophistication and generally provided limited detail on interaction quality, fidelity, or responsiveness
target_learning_goals: clinical communication skills
examples: The review reports many virtual patient systems relied on predefined response options with limited interaction flexibility, while only a small number of studies incorporated typed or voice-based natural language input

The first tier is multiple choice and the second tier is open-ended, giving "opportunity to students for free writing about the reason of the choice made in the first tier". Each question scores up to four points (one for the correct choice, three for a scientifically accurate explanation), for a maximum of 136 points. Reliability (cronbach alpha) was calculated as 0,87 and inter-rater Cohen's Kappa as 0,92.
requirements: Scoring categories adapted from Marek (1986): SU, PU, PUSAC, SAC, IEU, RO, FMO, E
Expert review by four physics education experts plus language experts for face and content validity
constraints: Because the questions were two-tier, item analysis was not performed
target_learning_goals: diagnosing alternative conceptions about impulse, momentum and collisions
examples: Piloted with 55 PSTs; example items ask which ball breaks a glass and about momenta of two people on skateboards pushing apart

article_title: The Effect of Project-Based History and Nature of Science Practices on the Change of Nature of Scientific Knowledge
citation: Ayşe Sert Çıbık. (2016). The Effect of Project-Based History and Nature of Science Practices on the Change of Nature of Scientific Knowledge. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(4), 453-472.
title: Implicit approach to teaching nature of science
description: The implicit approach is an instructional stance holding that students' views about NOS improve through active participation in scientific activities rather than through direct instruction about NOS. The article describes it as based on the anticipation that "students can positively improve their views about NOS through their active participations in scientific activities", so that the nature of scientific knowledge develops automatically through research-inquiry practices and scientific process skills. The article positions project-based HNOS training as an instantiation of this approach.
requirements: Training practices focusing on research-inquiry process and scientific process skills must be actualized for the nature of scientific knowledge to develop
constraints: The article notes the approach's underlying argument is that no extra effort is needed for teaching NOS beyond participating in scientific research studies, a claim other cited work (Khishfe & Abd-El-Khalick, 2002) qualifies by finding explicitly addressed approaches more effective
target_learning_goals: understanding of the nature of science and nature of scientific knowledge
examples: The experimental group's History and Nature of Science course was taught through project activities including PBL practice steps plus discussion, question-answer and brainstorming over 14 weeks

article_title: From a Gloss to a Learning Tool: Does Visual Aids Enhance Better Sentence Comprehension?
citation: Takeshi Sato and Akio Suzuki. (2012). From a Gloss to a Learning Tool: Does Visual Aids Enhance Better Sentence Comprehension? EUROCALL Conference, Gothenburg, Sweden, Proceedings. https://research-publishing.net
title: Image schema as a mediator connecting the senses of polysemous prepositions
description: Drawing on Johnson (1987) and cognitive linguistics, the article treats image schemas as abstract, non-propositional patterns of experience that can serve as a mediator connecting the senses of a polysemous word. The schema reflects the prototypical sense but can be extended to other examples, so the image can cover all the senses. If learners understand the image schema as a medium of each sense, they could differentiate senses of other prepositions.
requirements: Schematic images with flexibility and changeability such as foregrounding, rotation and focusing, which implies simple images may be better than fixed live-motion images
constraints: Derived from cognitive linguistics; the article notes live-motion images might prevent learners from modifying the images due to their fixed configuration
target_learning_goals: Understanding meaning structures of polysemous spatial prepositions
examples: The study used schematic images of prepositions as visual glosses in both experimental dictionaries

article_title: Success for All: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Sarah Miller, Andy Biggart, Seaneen Sloan, Liam O'Hare. (2017). Success for All: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Implement structured whole-school literacy programmes with high fidelity, as schools delivering the programme as prescribed saw larger literacy gains
description: The report's process and fidelity findings indicate that structured programmes yield more benefit when delivered as the developers intended. Schools delivering SfA "as prescribed by the developers saw larger gains in children's literacy after two years than those that completed fewer aspects of the programme", and schools rated 'refined' for fidelity scored higher on end-of-Year-1 outcomes. The principle is to support full, high-quality implementation rather than partial or adapted delivery.
requirements: Ongoing developer support and training (in SfA, 16 days over two years) plus an in-school coordinator to help ensure optimal implementation
constraints: Some schools found the programme prescriptive and adapted content and delivery; fidelity ratings in this trial were made by SfA rather than independently, and the fidelity analysis is exploratory with small samples
target_learners: Primary school pupils, including those eligible for free school meals
target_learning_goals: Early literacy attainment
examples: SfA rated the quality of implementation of 15 intervention schools and only one reached the highest 'refined delivery' status after two years; fidelity was analysed by coding refined or refined/routine schools as 1 (n=7) versus routine or mechanical as 0 (n=8)

article_title: The Cognitive Processing Potential of Infants: Exploring the Impact of an Early Childhood Development Programme
citation: van Eeden, R. & van Vuuren, J., 2017, 'The cognitive processing potential of infants: Exploring the impact of an early childhood development programme', South African Journal of Childhood Education 7(1), a499. https://doi.org/10.4102/sajce.v7i1.499
title: Image-brain stimulation rationale for infant flashcard learning
description: The programme's theoretical basis, drawn from Doman and Doman (2005) and Shichida (1993), holds that the right brain or image brain, which the article says "is dominant between the ages of 0 and 3", allows immediate recall of information stored from flashcards, while the more logical left brain relies on repetition to absorb information. The intervention therefore presents number, shape and colour concepts in isolation and repetitively, aiming to strengthen synaptic connections during the first year of life, a period of exuberant synaptogenesis and overlapping sensitive periods.
requirements: Daily, consistent flashcard exposure over 2–3 months so that the left brain is engaged through repetition
constraints: The article presents this as the programme's underlying rationale rather than a claim tested directly in the study
target_learning_goals: quantity recognition and basic mathematics principles
visual and auditory stimulation at the sensory developmental stage
examples: Ten flashcards of shapes, colours or numbers are shown for approximately 2–3 seconds each, including dot cards for numbers 1–30 and concepts of addition, subtraction, multiplication, greater than and less than

article_title: Changing Mindsets: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Cinzia Rienzo, Heather Rolfe and David Wilkinson (NIESR). (2015). Changing Mindsets: Evaluation report and Executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Implicit theories of intelligence (growth vs fixed mindset)
description: The intervention was based on Dweck's theory of implicit theories of intelligence, which holds that it is the individual's belief about the nature of ability — 'mindset' — that predicts resilience and perseverance in the face of challenge and failure. The theory identifies "incremental theories (growth mindsets) or entity theories (fixed mindsets)": individuals with a growth mindset believe they can develop their intelligence, while those with a fixed mindset believe intelligence is innate. The report presents this as the theoretical basis for both interventions and for teacher praise of effort rather than innate ability.
requirements: Teachers and deliverers communicate messages about effort, strategy and the malleability of intelligence rather than fixed ability
constraints: The report notes it was unaware of any rigorous UK trials of the growth mindset approach prior to this evaluation
target_learning_goals: Academic attainment in English and maths
Beliefs about the malleability of intelligence
Resilience and perseverance in learning
examples: The pupil workshops taught about the malleable nature of intelligence across six sessions covering growth/fixed mindsets, types of language, spelling and maths strategy tasks, and hard work, effort and practice.

article_title: Group Dynamic Assessment of L2 Learners' Writing Abilities
citation: Karim Shabani. (2018). Group Dynamic Assessment of L2 Learners' Writing Abilities. Iranian Journal of Language Teaching Research 6(1), 129-149. http://ijltr.urmia.ac.ir
title: Implicit-to-explicit mediational strategy typology for group writing revision
description: The study developed a posteriori a typology of six G-DA mediational strategies arranged from most implicit to most explicit: identifying the source of error, narrowing down the location of error, raising students' awareness, nominating potential sources of error, proposing probable correct response, and offering correct response and explanation. Mediation starts at a highly strategic or implicit level and progressively becomes more specific until the intended response is reached, tuned to learners' emerging ZPDs.
requirements: The mediator must track learners' responsiveness and offer the minimum level of guidance required
constraints: The strategies were developed a posteriori following dialogic interactions between the mediator and learners in this classroom context
target_learners: L2 freshmen in a community college writing course
target_learning_goals: error detection and correction in L2 writing
movement toward independent performance
examples: Episode transcripts show the teacher beginning with questions like what is the verb of this sentence and only offering the correct form when collective scaffolding failed

article_title: Pedagogical Experience on Formation of Tolerant and Multicultural Consciousness of Students
citation: Evgeny A. Naumenko, Olga N. Naumenko. (2016). Pedagogical Experience on Formation of Tolerant and Multicultural Consciousness of Students. European Journal of Contemporary Education. https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2016.17.335
title: Form confessional tolerance through long-term immersion in a specialized ethno-confessional course under controlled group-composition conditions
description: The article's central design recommendation is that tolerance results are achieved through immersion of students in the content of a special course, with the article stating "Results can be achieved under certain pedagogical conditions and particularly using the effect of immersion of students in the content of a special «Religions of the region under study» course." The course ran 292 hours (144 class hours) over an annual cycle, was regular and obligatory, and used active forms with didactically activating elements. The authors frame this as usable in state programs for preventing ethnic and confessional contradictions and extremism.
requirements: The number of Muslim students in the group should be significantly less than 50% of its composition (preferably up to 25–30%)
A group of 8–15 people is seen the best possible
Classes should cover quite a long period of time (annual cycle), be regular and obligatory
Professors must be of high qualification and a certain authority, and should not be deeply religious; clergy should not teach confessional-cycle subjects
constraints: The approach is not very effective for students with a high level of religious addiction
It is cost-consuming in the extent and form present in the experiment
The methodology was insufficiently effective when used incidentally in another discipline with Muslims at 50% of the group
target_learners: University students aged 17–20 in Regional studies and humanities programs
target_learning_goals: Confessional and interethnic tolerance
Multicultural consciousness
Understanding of religions of the region
examples: The experiment introduced the course at the Tyumen State Academy of International Economics, Management and Law for Regional studies students, with visits to a mosque, Orthodox church, Catholic church, and synagogue, and study of the Quran, Torah and Bible

citation: Eda Vula, Rrezarta Avdyli, Valbona Berisha, Blerim Saqipi, Shpetim Elezi. (2017). The impact of metacognitive strategies and self-regulating processes of solving math word problems. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education. https://doi.org/10.26822/iejee.2017131886
title: Modified IMPROVE-based metacognitive instruction program for solving math word problems
description: The intervention, titled "Metacognitive instruction for solving math word problems", was based on the IMPROVE program of Mevarech & Kramarski (1997) and the SOLVE IT! cognitive model for self-correcting strategies (Montague et al., 2008). The article describes IMPROVE as "a multidimensional teaching method" with three components: facilitation of metacognitive strategy acquisition, learning in collaborative groups with diverse previous knowledge, and provision of rich corrective information focusing on lower and higher order cognitive processes. It was implemented over one month in four experimental classes.
requirements: Full-time class teachers were given specific instructions regarding the modus-operandi and the manner of intervention, and held regular planning meetings with researchers.
constraints: The intervention period was one month; the authors report this short engagement was insufficient to improve third graders' results.
target_learners: third- and fifth-grade elementary learners in Kosovo primary schools
target_learning_goals: math word problem solving achievement
metacognitive and self-regulating strategy use
examples: Twelve math word problems were compiled per test wave: eight with consistent language (four one-operation, four multi-operation) and four with inconsistent language, scored 2/1/0 points.

description: The article situates BEST in CLASS within implementation science, defined as the scientific study of methods to promote the systematic uptake of research findings and other evidence-based practices into routine practices. The framework seeks to explore and explain how and why interventions work in real-world contexts, and the authors argue the practice-based coaching model has significant applications within it. Maintenance data showing continued teacher use of practices one month after coaching ceased are offered as first-step implementation evidence.
requirements: Examination of maintenance of teacher effects and training of school personnel to implement the coaching model
constraints: Future work should examine maintenance farther into the future, e.g., 6 months
target_learners: Early childhood teachers in authentic classroom settings
target_learning_goals: Sustained uptake of evidence-based instructional practices
examples: The study measured implementation and maintenance of practices at post-test and approximately 4 weeks after coaching ended

learning awareness

title: Teachers should implement direct vocabulary learning strategies particularly at the early stages of vocabulary learning
description: The article recommends that teachers implement direct vocabulary learning strategies because of their easy and effective application particularly at the early stages of vocabulary learning. constraints: The article cautions that different results might be produced if the study is conducted with low or advanced level language learners
Because of the short duration of the research, cautions should be made about considering the better performance of one group as an indication of vocabulary acquisition

examples: Group A was trained through Structured Reviewing (reviewing materials at different intervals) and Using Mechanical Techniques (flashcards with new vocabulary on one side and the definition on the other) over 10 academic sessions

Teamwork structures for participating nurses

self-efficacy

title: Intervention mapping with a logic model of change linking knowledge, empathetic skills, and self-efficacy to helping intention

Empirical evidence, literature reviews, and user needs data to populate each IM step

Quality of life of cancer survivors was the ultimate goal but was not directly measured in the model
No specific performance objective or change objectives were established for environmental impact

target_learning_goals: Increase helping intention toward friends with cancer
Increase accurate knowledge of cancer and cancer survivors
Acquire empathetic coping strategies
examples: The team applied IM steps 1-4: needs assessment and logic model of the problem, logic model of change, program design from surveys and a CDSR search, and material production with expert panel and think-aloud refinement.

title: Favor instructional methods that facilitate implicit learning over detailed step-by-step protocols when teaching complex nursing psychomotor skills to novices
description: The article proposes that nursing skills can be acquired with minimal instructions instead of detailed multi-page protocols, because implicit methods reduce demands on verbal working memory and free cognitive space for simultaneous tasks such as patient communication. Students taught with an instruction card using implicit strategies showed at least comparable performance to protocol-taught students across three studies, and in Study 3 tended towards greater consistency when multitasking. The authors conclude that "instructional methods that facilitate implicit learning may be preferable, as students in the implicit group demonstrated at least comparable performance in all studies and tended towards greater consistency when multitasking."
requirements: Development of the minimal instruction card requires a task analysis with teachers, researchers and experts to determine skill goals and identify the essential success factors.
constraints: The article states there is also a time and place for explicit learning, and that advantages of implicit learning may be moderately sized and need larger samples to estimate effects more accurately.
The article states that integrating implicit learning into educational programs requires significant time and adaptation from teachers and students.
target_learners: novice nursing students in bachelor's nursing education
target_learning_goals: acquisition and transfer of complex psychomotor nursing skills such as bandaging, including performance under multitasking demands
examples: Students practiced bandaging with a 67-word schematic instruction card using an external focus ("cover the ankle"), analogy learning ("create a tube"), and were compared against students using a 308-word step-by-step protocol.

(2025). Teaching nursing skills without detailed protocols: effects of an implicit learning strategy in nursing education. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-025-10421-y

article_title: Comparison of the effectiveness of video and breastfeeding simulator support to mothers who could not breastfeed their babies in the neonatal intensive care unit: a randomized controlled study.
citation: Tetik Metin Hatice & Yiğit Feride. (2025). Comparison of the effectiveness of video and breastfeeding simulator support to mothers who could not breastfeed their babies in the neonatal intensive care unit: a randomized controlled study. BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12486698/
title: Information-motivation-behavioral skills (IMB) model as the framework for designing breastfeeding training for NICU mothers
description: The IMB (information-motivation-behavioral skills) model structures the training content in both intervention arms: it informs mothers about breastfeeding, motivates them toward breastfeeding behaviour, and builds the behavioural skills to acquire and maintain that behaviour. The article states: "Therefore, we designed an education method with video and simulator methods based on the information-motivation-behavioral skills (IMB) model [21]." The same components recur in the methods: "The aim of the trainings was to inform the mothers about breastfeeding (knowledge), to motivate them to establish breastfeeding behaviour with the trainings received (motivation) and to enable them to acquire and maintain breastfeeding behaviour (behavioural skills)."
requirements: Training content must address all three IMB components: information, motivation, and behavioral skills for breastfeeding
constraints: The model was applied to postpartum mothers of babies admitted to a neonatal unit who had no early skin-to-skin contact or breastfeeding and who resided in a mother hotel
target_learners: Postpartum mothers whose newborns are hospitalized in a neonatal intensive care unit
target_learning_goals: Breastfeeding knowledge, motivation, and behavioral skills; breastfeeding self-efficacy and mother–infant attachment
examples: Both the 45-min to 1-h video training and the wearable-simulator training of the same duration and content were built on the IMB components
